title: Systematic Tasting
description: A full, repeatable tasting method that ends in a conclusion about quality and readiness to drink.
L: Assess clarity, intensity and colour precisely
Use colour to estimate age and grape

Systematic tasting uses fixed words so notes can be compared. Clarity: clear or hazy. Intensity: pale, medium or deep. Colour: for whites, lemon-green, lemon, gold, amber or brown; for rosés, pink, salmon or orange; for reds, purple, ruby, garnet, tawny or brown. Look at the core and the rim separately.
Clear or hazy; pale, medium, deep

Deep colour in a young red suggests thick skins, like Syrah or Cabernet, or a warm climate. Pale colour suggests Pinot Noir, Grenache or Nebbiolo. A wide watery rim in a red shows age. In whites, gold can mean age, oak or sweetness; amber or brown suggests oxidation or deliberate oxidative ageing, as in Oloroso.
Colour hints at grape, climate and age
A young red is deep purple and nearly opaque. Which grape is most likely?
Syrah's thick skins give deep, dark colour. Pinot Noir, Nebbiolo and Grenache are all naturally paler.

Haze in a wine that should be clear can mean a protein or microbial problem, though some unfiltered wines are naturally slightly cloudy. Bubbles in a still wine may mean refermentation in bottle. Brown tones in a young white suggest oxidation. Tartrate crystals and red sediment are harmless.
Haze or browning can warn of faults
A gold colour in a white wine always means the wine is old.
Not true. Gold can come from age, but also from oak ageing, a warm climate, sweetness or long skin contact. Look for other clues.
Use fixed terms for clarity, intensity and colour
Deep colour suggests thick skins or warmth; pale suggests thin skins
Haze, browning or bubbles in a still wine can signal a fault
Judge aroma intensity on a fixed scale
Judge development from youthful to tired
Check a wine is sound before tasting

First check the wine is clean, with no faults like cork taint or vinegar. Then judge intensity: light, medium minus, medium, medium plus or pronounced. Intensity depends on the grape, aromatic varieties like Muscat score high, and on concentration, which often reflects yield and vineyard quality.

Development tells you where the wine is in its life. Youthful wines show mainly primary and secondary aromas. Developing wines start to show tertiary notes, like dried fruit or leather. Fully developed wines are dominated by tertiary aromas. Past its best, the wine smells tired, with fading fruit and oxidised notes.
Match each description to its stage of development.
The balance between primary and tertiary aromas tells you how far along the wine is.
Smell the wine before swirling, then after. The first sniff catches the lightest aromas; swirling brings up the heavier ones. Comparing the two often reveals more.
A wine smells mostly of fresh blackberry and vanilla, with no tertiary notes. How would you describe its development?
Fresh fruit and oak, without tertiary notes, signal a youthful wine.
Check the wine is clean before judging intensity
Intensity runs from light to pronounced
Development moves from youthful to fully developed, then tired
Link aromas to grapes, climate and winemaking

Primary aromas come from the grape and fermentation. Group them: floral, like rose and violet; green fruit, like apple and pear; citrus; stone fruit, like peach; tropical; red fruit; black fruit; dried fruit; herbaceous, like grass and green pepper; herbal, like mint and eucalyptus; spice, like black pepper; and others, like wet stone.

Fruit families point to ripeness: green and citrus fruit for cool climates, tropical and jammy black fruit for warm ones. Herbaceous notes from pyrazines suggest Sauvignon Blanc or Cabernet family grapes. Black pepper from rotundone suggests Syrah. Secondary aromas, like butter or vanilla, reveal winemaking; tertiary ones reveal age.
Match each aroma to what it most likely reveals.
Each aroma is a clue about grape, place or process.

Start broad, then narrow. Fruit? Black fruit? Blackcurrant or blackberry? Fresh, ripe or cooked? Precise words help: fresh blackcurrant suggests a cooler Cabernet; jammy blackberry suggests a warmer region. Note several families, not just one.
Broad, then narrow, then ripe or fresh
Which aromas suggest a cool climate?
Fresh, tart fruit suggests cool conditions. Jammy and dried fruit point to heat or age.
Sort aromas into families before naming specifics
Fruit families reveal ripeness; specific aromas reveal grapes
Precise words, like fresh or jammy, add evidence
Judge sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body
Describe tannin by level and nature

On the palate, judge sweetness from dry to luscious; acidity from low to high; tannin from low to high; alcohol from low to high; body from light to full. For still wines, alcohol is low below 11%, medium from 11 to 13.9%, high from 14%. Each measure stands on its own, so judge them separately.

Tannin has a level and a nature. Ripe tannins feel soft, fine-grained and velvety. Unripe tannins feel green, coarse and astringent. Oak tannins can feel dry and grainy. Tannin also interacts: high acidity makes tannin feel harsher; sugar and alcohol make it feel softer.
Ripe tannin is soft; unripe tannin is coarse
Which element tends to make tannin feel harsher?
Acidity sharpens the perception of tannin. Sugar and alcohol soften it.

Sweetness can mask acidity, so a sweet Riesling may seem less acidic than it is. Alcohol adds body and can taste sweet. Carbon dioxide adds freshness. Judge each element on its own scale, then consider balance: do they support each other, or does one stick out?
Elements mask and support each other
For still wines, alcohol of 14% or more is described as ____.
14% and above is high; 11 to 13.9% medium; below 11% low.
Judge sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body separately
Tannin has a level and a nature, ripe or green
Elements interact: sugar masks acid, acid sharpens tannin
Confirming the nose and measuring length
Compare flavours on the palate with the nose

Flavour on the palate usually confirms the nose, but not always. Some wines show more on the palate than the nose, a sign of concentration. Judge flavour intensity from light to pronounced, and list the flavour families as for the nose. Retronasal smell, through the back of the throat, is doing most of the work.

After swallowing or spitting, count how long the flavours stay: short, under 5 seconds; medium, about 5 to 10; long, above 10. Only pleasant flavours count; a lingering bitterness or burn doesn't. Length is closely linked to concentration and ripeness, and is a strong sign of quality.
After spitting, the fruit flavour lasts about 12 seconds. How would you describe the finish?
Above 10 seconds of pleasant flavour is a long finish, a sign of quality.
Count the finish silently with each wine you taste for a week. You'll quickly calibrate what short, medium and long really mean.
A lingering bitter aftertaste counts towards a long finish.
Not true. Only pleasant flavours count. Bitterness or alcoholic burn that lingers is a sign of imbalance, not length.
Palate flavours usually confirm the nose
Judge flavour intensity like aroma intensity
Count pleasant flavour after swallowing: over 10 seconds is long
Decide whether a wine is ready to drink

Quality can be judged with four criteria, often remembered as BLIC: balance, length, intensity and complexity. A wine with all four is outstanding; with three, very good; two, good; one, acceptable. Faulty wines are poor. This avoids judging by personal taste alone.

Readiness asks whether the wine will improve. A wine with high concentration, firm tannin or acidity and youthful aromas may gain complexity with time. A wine already fully developed, or light and fruity, should be drunk now. Wines past their best are too old. Grape, region and vintage help you decide.
Match each BLIC criterion to what it asks.
Together they judge quality without relying on personal taste.

A full conclusion states quality and readiness, with reasons. For example: Very good. Balanced, with high acidity matched by intense fruit, a long finish, but limited complexity. Can drink now, but has potential for ageing. Reasons make your conclusion useful to others and to your future self.
Which features suggest a wine has potential for ageing?
Fully developed aromas suggest the wine is already at its peak.
Judge quality by balance, length, intensity and complexity
Concentration plus structure suggests ageing potential
Use precise scales for each element
Put the stages of systematic tasting in order.
Each stage gathers evidence for the next.
A white is deep gold, with honey and dried apricot aromas and a long finish. What do these clues suggest?
A white with age or botrytis
Deep gold, honey and dried fruit point to age, oak or noble rot.
Which are criteria in the BLIC quality check?
BLIC is balance, length, intensity and complexity. Colour belongs to appearance, and price says nothing about what is in the glass.
High acidity can make tannins feel harsher.
Yes. Acid and tannin together feel firmer; sugar and alcohol soften them.
A finish lasting under 5 seconds is ____.
Short is under 5 seconds; medium about 5 to 10; long over 10.
Appearance, nose, palate and conclusion, every time
Use fixed scales for intensity, structure and finish
Aromas are evidence of grape, climate, winemaking and age
Quality comes from balance, length, intensity and complexity
